LITERATURE REVIEW The global electricity consumption of data centers is becoming very relevant to the economy as accounted for approximately 3% of global electricity consumption in 2019, highlighting the significant economic impacts of these facilities [1]. Data centers are power-intensive buildings that include a variety of IT equipment. The conversion of electrical energy to heat energy by this equipment necessitates efficient cooling solutions to prevent thermal conditions that could lead to component and server shutdown or failure. The primary goal of a typical data center cooling systems is to remove excess heat and maintain optimal temperature and humidity levels to ensure uninterrupted and reliable operation of the equipment. Excess heat can damage IT and electrical equipment, leading to malfunctions, increased operational costs from equipment repairs or replacements, and heightened risk of fire and other safety issues [2]. The effectiveness of heat dispersion in data centers is crucial for the dependable, safe, and efficient functioning of data processing equipment. Consequently, a high-efficiency cooling system is essential [3]. In other words, without proper cooling, the risk of hardware failure escalates, underscoring cooling’s essential role in ensuring the continuous and reliable operation of servers in data centers [4]. In early data center facilities, air-cooled units were the standard for cooling. This method, although straightforward, was not particularly energy efficient [5], with waste of energy up to 70%. As the need for more efficient cooling grew, the industry developed advanced air cooling techniques such as hot/cold aisle containment, which significantly improved efficiency by strategically directing cool air to server intakes and channeling warm air away [6]. The so called “free-cooling” also emerged as a method that leveraged external environmental conditions (cold weather) to assist in cooling. This approach gained popularity, especially with data centers located in cold climates. Modern free-cooling systems include sophisticated control systems to balance external and internal environmental conditions [7]. With the advent of high-performance computing and increasing heat dissipation needs (up to 100 W/cm2), the limitations of air cooling became evident, leading to the exploration of more efficient methods such as liquid cooling. Liquid cooling has emerged as a more efficient and cost-effective solution compared with air cooling. Its higher energy efficiency, smaller footprint, increased server reliability, and lower total cost of ownership have made it a favorable option [8]. Common liquid cooling includes direct-to-chip (DTC) and immersion cooling. DTC cooling uses noncontact methods like microchannel heat sinks or cold plates to replace traditional air-cooled systems, enhancing heat transfer [7]. A coolant distribution unit circulates chilled liquid to cool primarily the processors, while other components might still use air cooling.
